description: Memory is not a camera. Every memory is reconstructed. This is how the brain encodes, stores… and sometimes invents.

hero.hook: Remembering is not rereading a file. It's reconstructing a scene.

blocks.text: We often imagine memory as a hard drive: we record, we store, we reread. The brain doesn't work like that. Every time you remember, you **reconstruct** a scene from fragments.
It’s powerful…and fallible. Understanding this means understanding why we forget, why we make mistakes, and why we learn.

blocks.caption: Different areas of the brain handle different forms of memory.

blocks.text: First there is the [[Working memory]]: what you hold “in mind” for a few seconds, like a telephone number. It is limited, around **7 items** on average. Then, **long-term memory**: facts, memories of events, skills like riding a bike.

These systems do not all live in the same place in the brain. The **prefrontal cortex**, the front part of the brain behind the forehead, helps a lot with working memory. Other regions, such as the **neocortex**, the outer layer of the brain, store the long term.

blocks.caption: The hippocampus, a deep structure, helps form new memories.

blocks.text: For information to go from fragile to durable, the brain must strengthen connections between **neurons**, the nerve cells. We're talking about **consolidation**, the transformation of a recent memory into a lasting trace. A small structure called **seahorse**, shaped like a sea horse in the temporal lobe, plays a key role in memories of events.
Sleep, especially certain phases, helps to consolidate what we learned during the day. Revising then sleeping often works better than revising until 3 a.m.

A famous rule, linked to **researcher Donald Hebb**: neurons that fire together tend to connect stronger. In summary: “what lights together binds together”. This is the principle of **neuroplasticity**, the brain's ability to modify its connections.

When you recall a memory, it temporarily becomes **malleable**, editable. Details from the present can slip in. Then the brain stores it again. This is why two witnesses to the same accident can tell different versions.
We can even create **false memories**: scenes that we believe to be true, but which never took place, or not like that. The brain fills in the gaps with what it already knows.
If you remembered every unnecessary detail, you would be saturated. Forgetting helps us to generalize, to decide, to keep the essentials. A good memory sorts as much as it retains.
Memory is an active reconstruction, not a perfect recording. It relies on several systems, is consolidated especially during sleep, and can become distorted with each reminder.
